topic: Base effect: equal rises in a price index give a falling inflation rate

concepts.name: base year index = 100
concepts.prereq_recalled: price index (earlier videos): base year value is set to 100

concepts.name: index vs inflation reference year
concepts.prereq_recalled: price index is worked out against the base year

concepts.name: inflation rate formula
concepts.prereq_recalled: inflation is measured against the previous year

concepts.name: base effect
concepts.prereq_recalled: inflation rate formula with the previous year as the divisor

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook defines base effect first and then gives an example. Here the term is named only after the numbers have already shown the effect: base year = 100, cut to one month, index vs inflation reference years, the formula, equal rises giving a falling %, and only then the name. The puzzle comes before the label.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Strip the data to one row (January) and add one reference idea at a time until the effect appears in the numbers.

opening.what: Names base effect as the topic and moves straight into recalling that a base year index is 100, while a table column builds.

moves.what: Already studied: any base year's price index is taken as 100.
For CPI combined the base year is 2012.
Recalls that a price index is measured point to point.
Iska matlab: the same month of the base year is used for the month being calculated.
Because some items in the basket are seasonal, months must be matched.
Only January data, and openly hypothetical, to keep the calculation simple and keep focus on base effect.
Price index is against the base year, but inflation rate is against the previous year.
Reads the formula as a sentence: this year minus last year, divided by last year, times 100.
Even though the index rises by the same 10 every year, lekin the inflation rate keeps falling.
Iska matlab: even with 2012 as base, last year's price level strongly drives the inflation rate.

examples.what: CPI combined uses 2012 as its base year.
January index 100 (2012), 110, 120, 130 in the next three years; inflation comes out 10%, 9%, 8.3% (the % values are on screen only).

closing.what: Names base effect as the promo slides over and the table disappears; no recap, no real-world use.

narration.density: About 4 new ideas (base year = 100, point to point, inflation vs previous year, base effect) in about 120 s, about 2 per minute. Slow in the first minute (a static table), rushed at the end (the punchline numbers are never read).

talmel_summary: Labels (column years, Price Index, Inflation %) appear right on their spoken words, and the bracket notes and formula card repeat the speech as English text. The meaning-carrying numbers (10%, 9%, 8.3%) are on screen only while the voice says just 'keeps falling', and the key term is then named over a promo with the table gone, so speech and picture never meet at the punchline.

voice.notes: About 199 words per minute, flat explaining tone. 'Base year', 'previous year' and 'base effect' get the stress. Few numbers are read aloud ('100', '2012', 'plus 10'); the computed percentages never are. The formula is read as one long sentence. The only short pauses (about 0.5 s) come around the year list at 17-20 s.

game_ideas.player_does: Sets next January's price index each year by choosing how many points to add.
game_ideas.process_happens: A bar for last year's index (the divisor) grows under a smaller bar for the rise; the inflation % is worked out live and written under the year, the way the video's table does.
game_ideas.win: Meet missions such as 'keep inflation at exactly 10% for three years' (needs a bigger rise every year) or 'make inflation fall while the index still rises'.
game_ideas.lose: Adding a flat 10 points each year when 10% inflation was asked gives 10%, 9%, 8.3%, and the screen labels it: same rise, bigger base, smaller %.

game_ideas.player_does: Drags 'base year' and 'previous year' tags onto the Price Index row and the Inflation % row, then picks which cell is the divisor for each year's inflation.
game_ideas.process_happens: A correct pick draws the arc from the right cell, as in the video; a wrong pick computes the % against the base year and shows a much larger number.
game_ideas.win: All tags and divisors placed correctly.
game_ideas.lose: Using the base year as divisor gives 30% for 2015 instead of 8.3%, showing why the reference year matters.

notes_questions.q: Price index kis saal ke respect mein nikalta hai, aur inflation rate kis saal ke respect mein?
Index 100 se 110, 120, 130 hua: har saal inflation % kitna bana? Table banaiye.
Index har saal barabar badhe, phir bhi inflation % kyun ghatta hai? (base effect)
Point-to-point measure mein base year ka wahi mahina kyun lete hain?
CPI combined ka base year kaun sa hai?

checks_learned: Numbers that carry the punchline (here 10%, 9%, 8.3%) must be spoken or pointed at by the voice, not only appear on screen.
The term being defined must be named while its diagram is still on screen; no promo or end card may start before the term and its conclusion line are finished.
When a formula is read aloud, highlight each table cell as it is used and substitute real numbers at least once.
Flag any table that stays unchanged for more than about 20 s while the narration moves on.
In a cause-effect concept the cause must be said in one plain line (the same rise on a bigger base gives a smaller %), not left for the viewer to work out.

teaching_best.why: Says openly that the data is hypothetical and cut to one month only to keep the calculation simple, which tells the learner what to ignore.
The contrast 'index against the base year, inflation against the previous year' sets up the whole effect in two short notes.
Surprise framing: the index rises by the same 10 every year, yet inflation falls; the term then names a puzzle the learner has already felt.

teaching_weak.why: The formula is read as words for about 17 s with no substitution of the table's numbers.
10%, 9% and 8.3% are never spoken, and the reason (a bigger divisor each year) is never said in plain words.
Base effect is named while the promo covers the table; no recap and no real-world use of the idea.
